feed.title: Stat! · Learn
feed.subtitle: Plain-language guides to the reasoning, tests and anatomy behind Stat!'s daily medical puzzles.

entry.title: How a daily puzzle is built: the library, the draw and the fairness rules
entry.summary: Where Stat!'s puzzles come from: a curated library of 250 diseases and 349 structures, one shared draw per date, and the rules that keep each game fair.

entry.title: Reading lab results: what high, low and abnormal really mean
entry.summary: Where reference ranges come from, why one in twenty healthy people falls outside each of them, and how to read the common blood tests that show up in clinical cases.

entry.title: Thinking in organ systems, disease types and acuity
entry.summary: How medicine sorts diseases by body system, by underlying mechanism and by time course, and why those three labels cut a long list of possibilities down so quickly.

entry.title: Classic clinical associations: findings that point to one disease
entry.summary: Some findings travel together so reliably that they suggest a diagnosis almost on sight. A tour of the classic pairings, and the traps where one finding fits several diseases.

entry.title: The clinical workup: from first complaint to diagnosis
entry.summary: How clinicians turn a presenting complaint into a diagnosis, with a focused history, a targeted examination and tests chosen to answer a question rather than to fish for one.

entry.title: Vital signs: the five numbers that frame every case
entry.summary: Temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate and oxygen saturation, with normal adult values, the patterns that matter, and why a trend beats a single reading.

entry.title: Imaging basics: X-ray, ultrasound, CT and MRI
entry.summary: What each imaging test is good at, what it costs in time and radiation, and how clinicians choose the right one for the question they are asking.

entry.title: Differential diagnosis: how clinicians narrow the possibilities
entry.summary: How to build a list of possible diagnoses, weigh how likely each one is, and pick the question or test that splits the list. The same logic solves Traits and Syndrome.

entry.title: Anatomical position, planes and directional terms
entry.summary: The shared vocabulary for describing where anything is in the body, from anatomical position and the three planes to pairs like anterior and posterior, medial and lateral, proximal and distal.

entry.title: Surface anatomy: finding the organs from the outside
entry.summary: The bony landmarks and simple rules of thumb clinicians use to locate the heart, lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, appendix and major pulses on the surface of the body.

entry.title: Why a daily puzzle helps you remember: retrieval, spacing and interleaving
entry.summary: Three well-studied learning effects explain why short daily practice beats cramming, and how to use Stat! alongside your other study.
